hook: Stuck on a puzzle? 'Can't do it' vs. 'Not yet'?  Which helps?
title: The Power of Yet

game.prompt: Scenario: You're trying to learn a new dance move.  Which thought helps you keep going?

choices.text: 'I can't do this. I'm just not good at dancing.'
'I can't do this *yet*. With more practice, I'll get it.'

game.reveal: Most people choose 'I can't do this yet'. That shift from 'can't' to 'not yet' opens up possibility. Carol Dweck, psychologist and author of *Mindset*, calls this the power of a growth mindset. Saying 'yet' signals that you believe your abilities are not fixed, but can be developed.

insight: Changing one word changes everything. 'Yet' acknowledges struggle while keeping hope alive.
model: When faced with a challenge, replace 'I can't' with 'I can't *yet*'. It shifts from limitation to potential.
try_today: Next time you feel stuck, say 'I can't do this yet.' and set a small step to get closer.

source.work: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006)

hook: You nailed that presentation! What made it click?
title: The Practice of Self-Reflection

game.prompt: Think about a recent success. What did you do *before* the success that contributed to it?

choices.text: I put in extra hours, even though I was tired.
I reviewed past mistakes and learned from them.

game.reveal: Most people pick 'luck' (choice 0). But Boyatzis & McKee say true success comes from a loop: learn, adjust, grow.  Choice 2 shows that mindset. It's not just about effort (choice 1), it's about reflecting on what worked and why.

insight: Self-reflection isn't just for failures. Analyzing successes reveals your strengths and how to repeat them.
model: The Self-Reflection Loop: Learn from both success and failure, adjust your approach, and keep growing.
try_today: After a win this week, write down 3 things you did that contributed to it.

source.work: Boyatzis & McKee, 'Resonant Leadership: Renewing the Power of Purpose in Organizations' (2014)

hook: Sandcastles: find the perfect balance of sturdiness and play.
title: Order & Chaos Balance

steps.scenario: You're building a sandcastle. Do you:

options.text: Carefully plan each turret, moat, and drawbridge.
options.feedback: Great for precision! But what if the tide comes in unexpectedly? Too rigid might miss the joy of improvisation.

options.text: Pile up sand randomly, see what emerges. Go with the flow!
options.feedback: Letting go can spark creativity and resilience! But a little structure keeps things from dissolving completely.

steps.scenario: Your friend's trying to organize their life:

options.text: Create a detailed schedule, color-coded by task.
options.feedback: A well-oiled machine? Maybe. But what if they miss a spontaneous concert or get stuck in one groove?

options.text: Encourage them to prioritize flexibility and say 'yes' to new things.
options.feedback: Balance allows for growth and unexpected joy! A little structure keeps things on track, but freedom lets life surprise you.

insight: Life thrives on both order and chaos. Too much of either stifles creativity and resilience. Aim for balance: a framework that allows for spontaneous beauty and joyful adaptation.
model: The sweet spot is the borderland where structure meets flow, rigidity embraces flexibility.
try_today: Pick one area of your life (work, hobbies, social) and identify one thing you could structure better, and one thing you could loosen up.

source.work: Peterson, *12 Rules for Life*; Tao Te Ching

try_team: Together, brainstorm one team rule that adds structure (clear deadlines) and one that embraces chaos (flexible meeting times). Experiment for a week!

hook: You're bored at work. What's your instinct?
title: Boredom Signal: Action or Insight?

steps.scenario: You're staring at spreadsheets, and the clock is moving glacially. Your mind wanders to that new game you want to try. What do you do?

options.text: Close your laptop and dive into the game!
options.feedback: It feels good in the moment, but tomorrow you'll likely feel more stressed about unfinished work. This is acting on the signal without understanding it.

options.text: Take a 5-minute walk. During that time, reflect: What am I actually bored *by*? Is there a better way to tackle this task?
options.feedback: This is turning the signal into insight! You're pausing to understand your boredom before reacting impulsively.

insight: Boredom signals a need for change. Don't react impulsively. Listen to it; thoughtful action leads to better outcomes.
model: Boredom signals: pause, reflect, then act.
try_today: Next time you feel bored, ask yourself: What am I avoiding? What could I do differently?

source.work: Danckert, J. D., & Mann, S. (2015). Boredom as a signal: The search for meaning in everyday life.
source.next_read: Chapter 6 of 'Bored To Death' by James Danckert and Sandi Mann (about 4 pages)

hook: You see your friend making a bold, risky move online. What do you say?
title: Finding the Golden Mean in Social Media

steps.scenario: Your friend posts something controversial on social media. They seem confident, but it could backfire. You know they're passionate and often speak their mind, even if it rubs people the wrong way. What do you say?

options.text: ‘Wow, that’s really brave! I admire your courage to stand up for what you believe in.’
options.feedback: This is supportive but doesn’t address the potential downsides. It might encourage them to be even bolder without considering consequences.

options.text: ‘Whoa, that's a bit risky, don't you think? People could react negatively.’
options.feedback: This is cautious but might discourage their voice. It focuses on the potential for harm without acknowledging their passion.

options.text: 'I understand why you feel strongly about this. What are some ways we can make sure your message gets across clearly and respectfully?'
options.feedback: This balances support with a focus on communication and impact. It acknowledges their courage while encouraging thoughtful expression.

steps.scenario: How do you react if they get negative responses?

options.text: 'Just ignore them! Don't let haters bring you down.'
options.feedback: This might feel good in the moment, but ignoring doesn’t address the issue and could lead to more negativity.

options.text: 'I see that people are upset. Maybe we can find a way to talk about it constructively?'
options.feedback: This promotes open dialogue and understanding, even when there are disagreements. It encourages finding common ground.

insight: Golden Mean means balancing courage & caution socially. Support passions, but encourage thoughtful expression for deeper connections.
model: Social media's Golden Mean: Share your voice bravely, but mindfully respect others.
try_today: See a controversial post? Offer constructive feedback instead of just agreeing/disagreeing. Ask questions to spark thoughtful discussion.
try_team: Before going online with controversy, discuss potential reactions & constructive replies as a team. Share Golden Mean examples from real life.
